children: By Alexandra Bruell and Anne Steele
YouTube revolutionized how we watch videos. Now it is coming for our bookshelves.
The streaming platform, owned by Alphabet's Google, has had discussions with publishers in recent months about developing an audiobook feature, according to people familiar with the matter.
The offering could be ready next year, the people said.

YouTube has weighed bundling the product in its ad-free YouTube Premium service, which starts at $15.99 a month and includes access to music and videos, the people said. Like other streaming platforms vying for consumers' attention, YouTube has packaged offerings together to make lucrative subscriptions more appealing.
It isn't clear how the company would display the content and whether it would charge for access to individual books.

The audiobook venture would bring it into an already crowded category, currently dominated by Spotify and Amazon's Audible. But publishing-industry executives believe there is still an opportunity in tapping in to YouTube's massive audience and are eager to find a revenue-generating alternative to the glut of unauthorized audio versions of their books that now appear on the platform.

Audiobooks have been among the strongest segments of the book market in recent years, with revenue from digital audiobook sales topping $1 billion in 2025, according to the Association of American Publishers. That same format posted revenue of $265 million in 2016.
